transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

I'm here because... well, I guess I'm just spending too much time checking things. Like, um, door locks, or my revision notes, file dimensions at work... even just the dressing supplies in my bathroom. I just... I can't seem to stop or move on to the next thing until I've checked them enough times. It just takes up hours, and I have to do it until the... the feeling goes away.
When you're checking these things, do you have thoughts that come into your mind that you don't want or that upset you?

Yeah... um, I guess I do. It's... well, even after I know I’ve already cleaned a wound area, or... or reviewed a CAD file at work, this thought just keeps cutting in. 

Just... telling me I missed one tiny thing. And that because I missed it, it’s going to turn into an infection, or... a design mistake that ends up hurting someone. I try to tell myself it's fine, but... I just can’t reason it away.
Do these thoughts usually make you feel anxious or upset, like you have to act on them to prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah... I guess they do. It gets pretty bad. 

That's... that's why I end up losing so many hours to rechecking everything. The door locks, the files, my notes... like I said earlier. I just... I don't feel allowed to move on. I have to keep going through the exact same routine enough times until... well, until the anxiety finally drops.
Are these checking behaviors the main type of ritual or compulsion you feel driven to perform, or are there other types of repetitive behaviors or mental acts you also engage in to reduce anxiety?

Um... no, I think it's mostly just what I already said. The checking. 

I just... I lose hours going back over the door locks, or the file dimensions at work... the dressing supplies. It's just going through that same routine. I don't feel allowed to stop until the feeling drops. So... yeah, just that, really. I don't think there's anything else.
